title: Put each payment on the exchange's business day

blocks.text: A card processor settles with an exchange in Tokyo and totals its payments per business day of that exchange. The ledger API it reads still returns `java.util.Date`. Since part of the fleet moved to a data centre in São Paulo, the totals from those servers disagree with the exchange's for payments made in the evening there. One older caller passes, instead of a payment moment, the settlement day it read from a `DATE` column with `ResultSet.getDate`; its report has been crashing, and once fixed it must show the same day the column holds, on servers in any zone.

cases.says: payments made during the exchange's day are totalled under that day
the business day of a moment is the exchange's day, not the day in the zone the server runs in
a java.sql.Date passed in is accepted rather than failing as a java.util.Date method would
a java.sql.Date is read as the day it names, not as a moment shifted into the exchange's zone

origin.section: java.sql.Date Is a java.util.Date That Breaks Its Parent's Contract

concepts: A Date holds only milliseconds since the epoch; toString(), the field getters and a SimpleDateFormat without a zone use the JVM's default zone, so the day of a Date depends on the zone you name.

java.sql.Date extends java.util.Date but throws from toInstant() and the time getters, so code written for java.util.Date fails on values from ResultSet.getDate; a java.sql.Date names a day, read with toLocalDate(), not by shifting its milliseconds into another zone.
